gd.enable_tbl_preview(n_head=8, n_tail=3)

A path is a sequence of edges leading from one node to another, and the length of the shortest
one is the distance between them. Paths are behind route planning, the chains of contacts that link
two people, the spread of a failure through a network, and many measures built on top of them,
from closeness centrality to the diameter. EdgeCase has methods for most of the standard path
problems:

| Question | Methods |
|---|---|
| What is the shortest route from A to B? | [`shortest_path()`](../reference/Graph.shortest_path.qmd), [`shortest_path_length()`](../reference/Graph.shortest_path_length.qmd), [`all_shortest_paths()`](../reference/Graph.all_shortest_paths.qmd) |
| How far is everything from A? | [`single_source_shortest_path_length()`](../reference/Graph.single_source_shortest_path_length.qmd), [`multi_source_shortest_path_length()`](../reference/Graph.multi_source_shortest_path_length.qmd) |
| How far is everything from everything? | [`all_pairs_shortest_path_length()`](../reference/Graph.all_pairs_shortest_path_length.qmd), [`floyd_warshall()`](../reference/Graph.floyd_warshall.qmd), [`johnson()`](../reference/Graph.johnson.qmd) |
| What are the next-best routes? | [`k_shortest_paths()`](../reference/Graph.k_shortest_paths.qmd), [`shortest_simple_paths()`](../reference/Graph.shortest_simple_paths.qmd), [`all_simple_paths()`](../reference/Graph.all_simple_paths.qmd) |
| What if some weights are negative? | [`bellman_ford_shortest_path()`](../reference/Graph.bellman_ford_shortest_path.qmd), [`find_negative_cycle()`](../reference/Graph.find_negative_cycle.qmd) |
| What route covers every edge, or every node? | [`eulerian_circuit()`](../reference/Graph.eulerian_circuit.qmd), [`traveling_salesman()`](../reference/Graph.traveling_salesman.qmd) |
| What is the cheapest way to connect some nodes? | [`steiner_tree()`](../reference/Graph.steiner_tree.qmd) |

[Traversals](09-traversals.qmd) covers the related questions of what a node can reach and how far
away it is in steps, and [Structural properties](11-structure.qmd#distances) covers the
whole-graph summaries of distance, such as the diameter.

## A road network

The examples on this page use a small network of roads between fourteen European cities. Each
road's weight is its length in kilometers. The cities also carry their latitude and longitude,
and a `pos` attribute that holds the two as an `(x, y)` pair, so that the network can be drawn as
a map:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec

cities = {
    "Amsterdam": (52.37, 4.90), "Brussels": (50.85, 4.35), "Paris": (48.86, 2.35),
    "Lyon": (45.76, 4.84), "Marseille": (43.30, 5.37), "Geneva": (46.20, 6.14),
    "Zurich": (47.37, 8.54), "Milan": (45.46, 9.19), "Munich": (48.14, 11.58),
    "Frankfurt": (50.11, 8.68), "Cologne": (50.94, 6.96), "Berlin": (52.52, 13.40),
    "Prague": (50.08, 14.44), "Vienna": (48.21, 16.37),
}

roads = [
    ("Amsterdam", "Brussels", 210), ("Amsterdam", "Cologne", 260), ("Amsterdam", "Berlin", 655),
    ("Brussels", "Paris", 300), ("Brussels", "Cologne", 210), ("Paris", "Lyon", 465),
    ("Paris", "Frankfurt", 570), ("Lyon", "Marseille", 315), ("Lyon", "Geneva", 150),
    ("Geneva", "Zurich", 280), ("Geneva", "Milan", 320), ("Marseille", "Milan", 600),
    ("Zurich", "Milan", 280), ("Zurich", "Munich", 315), ("Zurich", "Frankfurt", 410),
    ("Cologne", "Frankfurt", 190), ("Frankfurt", "Munich", 390), ("Frankfurt", "Berlin", 545),
    ("Berlin", "Prague", 350), ("Munich", "Prague", 380), ("Munich", "Vienna", 435),
    ("Prague", "Vienna", 330), ("Munich", "Milan", 490),
]

places = [(city, {"lat": lat, "lon": lon, "pos": [lon, lat]}) for city, (lat, lon) in cities.items()]
road_net = ec.Graph.from_edges(roads, nodes=places, graph_name="Roads")
road_net
```

Since the edges have weights, `from_edges()` made the graph weighted. As on the
[Traversals](09-traversals.qmd) page, a small helper turns the node IDs that path methods return
into city names:

```{python}
def names(ids):
    return [road_net.get_label_from_id(i) for i in ids]
```

To label each road with its length in the drawing, the length must also be stored as an edge
attribute, since `edge_label_by=` reads attributes and the weight is a separate field. The
`pos` attribute then serves as the layout:

```{python}
road_net.set_edge_attrs("km", {e["id"]: e["weight"] for e in road_net.get_edge_df().iter_rows(named=True)})
road_net.plot(layout="pos", label_by="label", edge_label_by="km", node_size=10, height=480)
```

## The shortest path between two nodes

[`shortest_path()`](../reference/Graph.shortest_path.qmd) finds a shortest path from one node to
another, and [`shortest_path_length()`](../reference/Graph.shortest_path_length.qmd) finds its
length without building the path. With `return_list=True`, `shortest_path()` returns the path as a
list of node IDs:

```{python}
names(road_net.shortest_path("Amsterdam", "Vienna", return_list=True))
```

```{python}
road_net.shortest_path_length("Amsterdam", "Vienna")
```

The fastest way from Amsterdam to Vienna is south-east through Germany, a drive of 1275 km.

### What "shortest" means

On a weighted graph, the shortest path is the one with the lowest total weight, found with
Dijkstra's algorithm. On an unweighted graph, it is the one with the fewest edges, found with a
breadth-first search, and any weights are ignored. The same roads give a different answer when the
graph is built with `weighted=False`:

```{python}
hops = ec.Graph.from_edges(roads, nodes=places, weighted=False)
names(hops.shortest_path("Amsterdam", "Vienna", return_list=True)), hops.shortest_path_length("Amsterdam", "Vienna")
```

The route through Berlin and Prague has only three legs, one fewer than the route through Germany,
but it is 60 km longer. Which answer is right depends on the question: hops suit networks where
every link costs the same, such as the steps between people in a social network, and weights suit
networks where links differ, such as roads, flights, or the latency of network connections. (The
nodes were created in the same order in both graphs, so they have the same IDs, and the `names()`
helper works for both.)

In a weighted graph, an edge without a weight counts as 1. In a directed graph, paths follow edge
direction, so the distance from A to B can differ from the distance from B to A, or one of them may
not exist at all.

### Storing a path

Without `return_list=True`, `shortest_path()` follows the convention of the other algorithms and
stores its result on the graph. Each node on the path gets its position along it, counted from 0,
in a `shortest_path_order` attribute (or the name given by `attr_name=`), and every other node gets
a null value:

```{python}
(
    road_net
    .shortest_path("Amsterdam", "Vienna")
    .get_node_df()
    .select("label", "shortest_path_order")
    .drop_nulls()
    .sort("shortest_path_order")
)
```

A stored path is easy to highlight in a drawing. Since `color_by=` gives each distinct value its own
color, a simple flag on the nodes of the path works better than their positions:

```{python}
route = road_net.shortest_path("Amsterdam", "Vienna", return_list=True)
road_net.set_node_attrs("on_route", {node: True for node in route})
road_net.plot(layout="pos", color_by="on_route", label_by="label", edge_label_by="km", node_size=10, height=480)
```

The edges whose two ends are both on the route take the route's color, so the drive stands out
from the rest of the network.

When no path exists, `shortest_path()` and `shortest_path_length()` return `None`. Because of this,
a chain such as `graph.shortest_path(a, b).plot()` fails when `b` can't be reached from `a`, so
check with [`has_path()`](../reference/Graph.has_path.qmd) first when that might happen.

### Ties

There is often more than one shortest path, especially when distances are counted in hops.
`shortest_path()` returns one of them, and [`all_shortest_paths()`](../reference/Graph.all_shortest_paths.qmd)
returns them all. In the karate club, member `"11"` (ID 12) has only one friend, the instructor,
and is three steps from the administrator (ID 34) by any of four routes:

```{python}
karate = ec.karate_club()
karate.all_shortest_paths(12, 34)
```

Every route runs through the instructor and then through one of the four friends that the
instructor and the administrator have in common. Counting how many shortest paths pass through each
node is the idea behind betweenness centrality (see [Centrality](13-centrality.qmd)). On a large
graph the number of ties can be very large, and `max_paths=` caps it.

## Choosing an algorithm

`shortest_path()` uses Dijkstra's algorithm on weighted graphs, which is the right choice for most
work. A few alternatives are faster in particular situations, or handle cases that Dijkstra's
algorithm can't:

| Method | Algorithm | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| [`shortest_path()`](../reference/Graph.shortest_path.qmd) | Dijkstra, or breadth-first search when unweighted | the weights are non-negative (the usual case) |
| [`bidirectional_dijkstra()`](../reference/Graph.bidirectional_dijkstra.qmd) | Dijkstra from both ends at once | a single long path is needed in a large graph |
| [`astar_path()`](../reference/Graph.astar_path.qmd), [`astar_path_length()`](../reference/Graph.astar_path_length.qmd) | A* search, guided by an estimate of the remaining distance | a good estimate is available, as on maps and grids |
| [`bellman_ford_shortest_path()`](../reference/Graph.bellman_ford_shortest_path.qmd) | Bellman-Ford | some weights are negative |
| [`goldberg_radzik()`](../reference/Graph.goldberg_radzik.qmd) | Goldberg-Radzik | some weights are negative, and all distances from a source are needed |
| [`ada_star_search()`](../reference/Graph.ada_star_search.qmd) | Anytime Dynamic A* | a good path is needed quickly, and can be improved later |

[`bidirectional_dijkstra()`](../reference/Graph.bidirectional_dijkstra.qmd) grows a search from
each end and stops when the two meet, which usually explores far fewer nodes than a search from one
end. It returns the length and the path together:

```{python}
road_net.bidirectional_dijkstra("Amsterdam", "Vienna")
```

### A* search

A* search is Dijkstra's algorithm steered by a *heuristic*, a function that estimates the remaining
distance from any node to the target. The search explores the nodes that look closest to the target
first, so with a good estimate it finds the same shortest path after looking at far fewer nodes.
The estimate must never be larger than the true distance, or the path found may not be the
shortest.

For a road network, the straight-line distance between two cities is the natural estimate, since
no road is shorter than the straight line. The heuristic receives two node IDs, the current node
and the target, and here computes the great-circle distance between them from their stored
coordinates:

```{python}
import math


def straight_line(node, target):
    a = road_net.get_node(node).attributes
    b = road_net.get_node(target).attributes
    lat1, lat2 = math.radians(a["lat"]), math.radians(b["lat"])
    dlat, dlon = lat2 - lat1, math.radians(b["lon"] - a["lon"])
    h = math.sin(dlat / 2) ** 2 + math.cos(lat1) * math.cos(lat2) * math.sin(dlon / 2) ** 2
    return 2 * 6371 * math.asin(math.sqrt(h))


names(road_net.astar_path("Amsterdam", "Vienna", heuristic=straight_line))
```

A* found the same route as Dijkstra's algorithm, as it must. On fourteen cities the saving is
negligible, but on a road network of millions of junctions it is large, which is why A* and its
relatives are the standard algorithms for route planning.

When the nodes have no coordinates, [`alt_heuristic()`](../reference/Graph.alt_heuristic.qmd)
builds a heuristic from the graph itself. It picks a few *landmark* nodes, computes the distance
from each to every node in advance, and uses the triangle inequality to bound the remaining
distance. The precomputation pays off when many paths are needed on the same graph:

```{python}
grid = ec.power_grid()
landmarks = grid.alt_heuristic(k=8, seed=1)
grid.astar_path_length(1, 4000, heuristic=landmarks), grid.shortest_path_length(1, 4000)
```

The heuristic is built from the graph as it is, so rebuild it after the graph changes.

## Negative weights

Dijkstra's algorithm assumes that weights are never negative, and the methods that use it raise a
`ValueError` when they find a negative weight. Negative weights are rare in physical networks, but
they arise naturally when a weight represents a gain as well as a cost. The classic example is
currency exchange. Converting one currency to another multiplies an amount by an exchange rate, and
taking the logarithm turns that product into a sum, so with each rate stored as `-log(rate)`, the
shortest path is the conversion that ends with the most money.

Here a dealer quotes each conversion at the market rate less a spread, which is small for the most
traded pairs of currencies and larger for the others. Some of the weights come out negative:

```{python}
usd_value = {"USD": 1.0, "EUR": 1.08, "GBP": 1.27, "JPY": 0.0067, "CHF": 1.13}
spreads = {
    ("USD", "EUR"): 0.001, ("USD", "GBP"): 0.002, ("EUR", "GBP"): 0.002,
    ("USD", "JPY"): 0.002, ("EUR", "CHF"): 0.002, ("EUR", "JPY"): 0.004,
    ("GBP", "CHF"): 0.008, ("CHF", "JPY"): 0.015,
}


def quote(have, want):
    spread = spreads.get((have, want), spreads.get((want, have)))
    return usd_value[have] / usd_value[want] * (1 - spread)


fx = ec.Graph.from_edges(
    [
        (x, y, -math.log(quote(x, y)), {"rate": quote(x, y)})
        for a, b in spreads
        for x, y in [(a, b), (b, a)]
    ],
    directed=True,
    graph_name="Currency exchange",
)
fx.get_edge_df().head(4)
```

[`bellman_ford_shortest_path()`](../reference/Graph.bellman_ford_shortest_path.qmd) handles
negative weights. It always uses the weights, and otherwise works like `shortest_path()`. The best
way to turn Swiss francs into yen is not the direct quote, with its wide spread, but a chain of
conversions through the euro and the dollar:

```{python}
fx_names = lambda ids: [fx.get_label_from_id(i) for i in ids]
fx_names(fx.bellman_ford_shortest_path("CHF", "JPY", return_list=True))
```

[`goldberg_radzik()`](../reference/Graph.goldberg_radzik.qmd) computes the distance from one node
to every other in a graph with negative weights. It returns a predecessor and a distance for each
node, and converting the distance back with `exp(-distance)` gives the best rate. Applied to 1000
francs, the chain gains about 1700 yen over the direct quote:

```{python}
predecessors, distances = fx.goldberg_radzik("CHF")
jpy = fx.get_id_from_label("JPY")
round(1000 * math.exp(-distances[jpy])), round(1000 * quote("CHF", "JPY"))
```

### Negative cycles

Shortest paths are only defined when no cycle has a negative total weight, since otherwise going
round the cycle again always makes a path shorter. With exchange rates, a negative cycle is an
*arbitrage*: a sequence of conversions that ends with more money than it began with. The dealer's
spreads rule that out, but a second dealer who quotes pounds into yen 1% above the market rate
creates one:

```{python}
mispriced = usd_value["GBP"] / usd_value["JPY"] * 1.01
fx.add_edge("GBP", "JPY", weight=-math.log(mispriced), rate=mispriced, rel="mispriced")
fx.negative_edge_cycle()
```

[`negative_edge_cycle()`](../reference/Graph.negative_edge_cycle.qmd) reports whether any negative
cycle exists, and [`find_negative_cycle()`](../reference/Graph.find_negative_cycle.qmd) finds one
that can be reached from a given node, as a list of nodes that ends where it began:

```{python}
cycle = fx.find_negative_cycle("USD")
fx_names(cycle)
```

Converting dollars to pounds, pounds to yen at the mispriced rate, and yen back to dollars returns
about 0.6% more than it started with. With the cycle in the graph, `bellman_ford_shortest_path()`
raises a `ValueError` rather than return a meaningless path.

In an undirected graph, every edge can be crossed in both directions, so a single negative edge is
already a negative cycle. Negative weights are therefore only meaningful in directed graphs.

## From one node to many

Many questions need the distance from one node to every other: how far is each city from the
warehouse, how many steps is each person from the source of a rumor?
[`single_source_shortest_path_length()`](../reference/Graph.single_source_shortest_path_length.qmd)
answers them with a single search, and stores each node's distance in an attribute named after the
method:

```{python}
(
    road_net
    .single_source_shortest_path_length("Paris")
    .get_node_df()
    .select("label", "single_source_shortest_path_length")
    .sort("single_source_shortest_path_length")
)
```

With `cutoff=`, the search stops at a given distance, and with `return_dict=True` the method returns
a dictionary of the nodes it reached. These are the cities within 600 km of Paris:

```{python}
sorted(names(road_net.single_source_shortest_path_length("Paris", cutoff=600, return_dict=True)))
```

[`single_source_shortest_path()`](../reference/Graph.single_source_shortest_path.qmd) returns the
paths themselves, as a dictionary from each reached node to a path that leads to it. Together the
paths form a *shortest-path tree*, which is a compact routing table for everything that starts at
the source:

```{python}
from_paris = road_net.single_source_shortest_path("Paris")
names(from_paris[road_net.get_id_from_label("Vienna")])
```

The methods for a single target work the other way round, finding the distance or path from every
node *to* the target. In an undirected graph that's the same thing, but in a directed graph, such
as a network of one-way streets, it isn't.

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| [`single_source_shortest_path_length()`](../reference/Graph.single_source_shortest_path_length.qmd), [`single_source_shortest_path()`](../reference/Graph.single_source_shortest_path.qmd) | the distance or a path from a source to every reachable node |
| [`single_target_shortest_path_length()`](../reference/Graph.single_target_shortest_path_length.qmd), [`single_target_shortest_path()`](../reference/Graph.single_target_shortest_path.qmd) | the distance or a path to a target from every node that can reach it |
| [`single_source_all_shortest_paths()`](../reference/Graph.single_source_all_shortest_paths.qmd) | every tied shortest path from a source to each node |
| [`predecessor()`](../reference/Graph.predecessor.qmd) | each node's predecessors on every shortest path from a source |
| [`multi_source_shortest_path_length()`](../reference/Graph.multi_source_shortest_path_length.qmd), [`multi_source_shortest_path()`](../reference/Graph.multi_source_shortest_path.qmd) | the distance or a path from the nearest of several sources |

### The nearest of several sources

[`multi_source_shortest_path_length()`](../reference/Graph.multi_source_shortest_path_length.qmd)
measures the distance from every node to whichever of several sources is nearest. It answers the
facility questions: how far is each customer from the closest warehouse, hospital, or server? With
warehouses in Paris, Berlin, and Milan, the distances and paths together show which warehouse
should serve each city:

```{python}
import polars as pl

depots = ["Paris", "Berlin", "Milan"]
km = road_net.multi_source_shortest_path_length(depots, return_dict=True)
paths = road_net.multi_source_shortest_path(depots)

pl.DataFrame({
    "city": names(paths),
    "depot": [road_net.get_label_from_id(path[0]) for path in paths.values()],
    "km": [km[node] for node in paths],
}).sort("depot", "km")
```

Each path starts at the nearest depot, so its first node identifies the depot that serves the city.
Vienna is the farthest city from any depot, 680 km from Berlin, which makes it the obvious place
for a fourth.

## Between every pair

[`all_pairs_shortest_path_length()`](../reference/Graph.all_pairs_shortest_path_length.qmd)
computes the distance between every pair of nodes, as a nested dictionary in which
`result[a][b]` is the distance from `a` to `b`. It is convenient to turn part of it into a
distance table:

```{python}
dist = road_net.all_pairs_shortest_path_length()

sample = ["Amsterdam", "Berlin", "Marseille", "Vienna"]
ids = [road_net.get_id_from_label(city) for city in sample]
pl.DataFrame({"from": sample} | {city: [dist[i][j] for i in ids] for city, j in zip(sample, ids)})
```

The table is symmetric because the roads are two-way. In a directed graph, `result[a][b]` and
`result[b][a]` can differ, and pairs that can't reach each other are left out rather than given an
infinite distance.

A full table has one entry per pair of nodes, so its size grows with the square of the number of
nodes: a graph of 100,000 nodes has ten billion pairs. For large graphs, compute distances from the
sources you actually need, or use a summary such as the [mean distance](11-structure.qmd#distances).

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| [`all_pairs_shortest_path_length()`](../reference/Graph.all_pairs_shortest_path_length.qmd), [`all_pairs_shortest_path()`](../reference/Graph.all_pairs_shortest_path.qmd) | the distance, or one shortest path, between every pair |
| [`all_pairs_all_shortest_paths()`](../reference/Graph.all_pairs_all_shortest_paths.qmd) | every shortest path between every pair |
| [`floyd_warshall()`](../reference/Graph.floyd_warshall.qmd) | the distances between every pair, allowing negative weights; best for small, dense graphs |
| [`johnson()`](../reference/Graph.johnson.qmd) | a shortest path between every pair, allowing negative weights; best for sparse graphs |
| [`metric_closure()`](../reference/Graph.metric_closure.qmd) | a complete graph, with an edge between every pair weighted by their distance |

`floyd_warshall()` and `johnson()` handle the currency graph, as long as there's no arbitrage
in it. Removing the mispriced quote restores that, and the best rate from pounds to every other
currency follows:

```{python}
fx.select_edges(lambda edge: edge.attributes.get("rel") == "mispriced").delete_edges_ws()
gbp = fx.get_id_from_label("GBP")
{fx.get_label_from_id(c): round(math.exp(-d), 4) for c, d in fx.floyd_warshall()[gbp].items()}
```

Converting pounds to francs through the euro gives a better rate than the direct quote, since the
two legs through the euro together cost less than the direct quote's wide spread.

## Alternative routes

The shortest path is often not the only route worth knowing. A backup is needed when the best route
is closed, and a choice of good routes spreads traffic. [`k_shortest_paths()`](../reference/Graph.k_shortest_paths.qmd)
returns the `k` shortest *simple* paths (paths that visit no node twice), each with its length:

```{python}
[(names(path), length) for path, length in road_net.k_shortest_paths("Amsterdam", "Vienna", k=4)]
```

The route through Berlin and Prague is only 60 km longer than the best route, which makes it a good
alternative. The third and fourth routes are small detours on the first.

[`shortest_simple_paths()`](../reference/Graph.shortest_simple_paths.qmd) produces the same
sequence lazily, computing each path only when it is asked for. Take as many as needed with
`itertools.islice()`, or stop at the first path that meets some condition, such as avoiding a city:

```{python}
import itertools

[names(path) for path in itertools.islice(road_net.shortest_simple_paths("Paris", "Milan"), 3)]
```

```{python}
milan_routes = road_net.shortest_simple_paths("Paris", "Milan")
next(names(path) for path in milan_routes if "Geneva" not in names(path))
```

If the road through Geneva is closed, the best way from Paris to Milan is through Frankfurt and
Zurich.

### Every simple path

[`all_simple_paths()`](../reference/Graph.all_simple_paths.qmd) lists every simple path
between two nodes, in no particular order. The number of simple paths grows explosively with the
size of a graph, so on anything beyond a small graph, set `cutoff=` to limit the number of edges
per path:

```{python}
short_routes = road_net.all_simple_paths("Paris", "Milan", cutoff=3)
len(road_net.all_simple_paths("Paris", "Milan")), [names(path) for path in short_routes]
```

Even in this small network, there are 119 ways to drive from Paris to Milan without passing through
any city twice, but only four of them use three roads or fewer.
[`all_simple_edge_paths()`](../reference/Graph.all_simple_edge_paths.qmd) lists the paths as edge
IDs instead, which tells parallel edges apart, and [`count_trails()`](../reference/Graph.count_trails.qmd)
and [`enumerate_trails()`](../reference/Graph.enumerate_trails.qmd) cover *trails*, which may revisit
a node but not an edge. [`is_simple_path()`](../reference/Graph.is_simple_path.qmd) checks a
sequence of nodes.

### Disjoint paths

Alternatives that share a road don't help when that road is closed.
[`edge_disjoint_paths()`](../reference/Graph.edge_disjoint_paths.qmd) finds the largest set of
paths that share no edge, and [`node_disjoint_paths()`](../reference/Graph.node_disjoint_paths.qmd)
the largest set that share no node other than their ends:

```{python}
[names(path) for path in road_net.node_disjoint_paths("Paris", "Vienna")]
```

There are only two, because Vienna has only two roads. The number of disjoint paths between two
nodes measures how robust the connection between them is, and
[Connectivity and flows](16-connectivity.qmd) builds on it.

## Walks

A *walk* is a sequence of edges that may revisit nodes and edges, and walks underlie several
measures that consider every route between two nodes rather than only the shortest.
[`count_walks()`](../reference/Graph.count_walks.qmd) counts the walks of a given length between
every pair of nodes. In the karate club, the walks of length two from the instructor to the
administrator are the routes through a common friend, and there are four of them, matching the
four common friends found on the [Traversals](09-traversals.qmd#neighbors) page:

```{python}
karate.count_walks(2)[1][34], karate.count_walks(3)[1][34]
```

[`random_walk()`](../reference/Graph.random_walk.qmd) takes a random walk from a node. On a weighted
graph, each step favors the heavier edges, so on the road network, where weights are lengths, the
walker prefers long roads. Use `seed=` for a repeatable walk:

```{python}
names(road_net.random_walk("Paris", steps=6, seed=3, return_list=True))
```

Random walks are the basis of PageRank (see [Centrality](13-centrality.qmd)), of the Walktrap and
Infomap community methods (see [Community detection](14-communities.qmd)), and of several
similarity measures (see [Similarity and link prediction](18-similarity.qmd)).
[`random_walk_with_restart()`](../reference/Graph.random_walk_with_restart.qmd),
[`random_edge_walk()`](../reference/Graph.random_edge_walk.qmd), and
[`generate_random_paths()`](../reference/Graph.generate_random_paths.qmd) are variations.

## Distance-based indices

A few single numbers summarize the distances of a whole graph. The best known is the *Wiener
index*, the sum of the distances between all pairs of nodes, which originated in chemistry as a
predictor of the boiling points of molecules:

```{python}
road_net.wiener_index(weighted=False), road_net.wiener_index()
```

[`wiener_index()`](../reference/Graph.wiener_index.qmd) sums the edge weights on a weighted graph,
and counts hops with `weighted=False`. Over the 91 pairs of cities, the hop
counts add up to 203, which is an average of 2.23 hops per pair, the
[mean distance](../reference/Graph.mean_distance.qmd). The road lengths add up to 71,360 km.
[`hyper_wiener_index()`](../reference/Graph.hyper_wiener_index.qmd) is a variant that
weights long distances more heavily.

### Resistance distance

The *resistance distance* treats a graph as an electrical circuit, with a one-ohm resistor on each
edge, and measures the resistance between two nodes. Unlike the shortest-path distance, it takes
every route into account: many parallel routes bring two nodes closer together, while a single
bridge between them keeps them apart. [`resistance_distance()`](../reference/Graph.resistance_distance.qmd)
computes it for one pair:

```{python}
round(karate.resistance_distance(1, 34), 3), round(karate.resistance_distance(1, 12), 3)
```

The instructor and the administrator are two steps apart, but because there are so many routes
between them, the resistance is only 0.254, a quarter of a single edge. Member `"11"` (ID 12), by
contrast, has a single friendship with the instructor, and the resistance across it is a full
1.0. [`resistance_distance_matrix()`](../reference/Graph.resistance_distance_matrix.qmd) computes
the resistance between every pair, and [`kirchhoff_index()`](../reference/Graph.kirchhoff_index.qmd)
sums it over all pairs, the electrical counterpart of the Wiener index.

## Routing problems

The last group of problems asks for a route with a property, rather than a route between two
nodes: one that covers every edge, one that visits every node, or a network that connects some
nodes as cheaply as possible.

### Eulerian paths and circuits

An *Eulerian circuit* is a closed walk that uses every edge exactly once, and an *Eulerian path* is
one that needn't return to its start. Graph theory began with the question of whether one exists
in the city of Königsberg, whose seven bridges joined two river banks and two islands (here the
north bank, the south bank, the central island, and the land to the east). Two pairs of places are
joined by two bridges each, so the graph has parallel edges:

```{python}
koenigsberg = ec.Graph.from_edges(
    [
        ("North", "Island"), ("North", "Island"),
        ("South", "Island"), ("South", "Island"),
        ("North", "East"), ("South", "East"), ("Island", "East"),
    ],
    graph_name="Königsberg",
)
bridges = koenigsberg.degrees(return_dict=True)
{koenigsberg.get_label_from_id(place): n for place, n in bridges.items()}
```

Euler showed in 1736 that a connected graph has an Eulerian circuit exactly when every node has an
even degree, and an Eulerian path exactly when no more than two nodes have an odd degree. Every
place in Königsberg has an odd number of bridges, so no walk crosses each bridge once.
[`is_eulerian()`](../reference/Graph.is_eulerian.qmd) and
[`has_eulerian_path()`](../reference/Graph.has_eulerian_path.qmd) make the two tests:

```{python}
koenigsberg.is_eulerian(), koenigsberg.has_eulerian_path()
```

[`is_semieulerian()`](../reference/Graph.is_semieulerian.qmd) checks for a path without a circuit,
and [`eulerian_circuit()`](../reference/Graph.eulerian_circuit.qmd) and
[`eulerian_path()`](../reference/Graph.eulerian_path.qmd) find the walk when one exists.

When none exists, [`eulerize()`](../reference/Graph.eulerize.qmd) adds the fewest duplicate edges,
or on a weighted graph the lightest ones, that make every degree even. The duplicates are the edges
that a closed walk must use twice, so this solves the *Chinese postman problem*: the shortest route
that covers every street at least once, as a postal worker or a snowplow must. The duplicates are
marked with an `eulerize_added` attribute:

```{python}
walkable = koenigsberg.eulerize()
walkable.get_edge_df().filter(eulerize_added=True)
```

```{python}
[walkable.get_label_from_id(node) for node in walkable.eulerian_circuit()]
```

Recrossing one of the bridges between the north bank and the island, and the bridge between the
south bank and the east, gives a walk over all seven bridges that crosses nine times. In a graph with
parallel edges, a list of nodes doesn't say which of two bridges was crossed;
`eulerian_path(edges=True)` returns edge IDs instead.

### The traveling salesperson problem

The traveling salesperson problem asks for the shortest round trip that visits every one of a set
of places. [`traveling_salesman()`](../reference/Graph.traveling_salesman.qmd) solves it on any
connected graph, not only on a complete one: between consecutive stops it travels along a shortest
path, so the route it returns may pass through places that aren't stops. Here a sales rep based in
Paris must visit Milan, Berlin, and Amsterdam:

```{python}
tour = road_net.traveling_salesman(nodes=["Paris", "Milan", "Berlin", "Amsterdam"])
names(tour)
```

The tour returns to Paris after passing through five other cities on the way. With `cycle=False`,
the method returns a one-way route instead, by dropping the most expensive leg of the round trip.

The problem is hard to solve exactly, so the method uses heuristics that give good, but not always
optimal, routes. The default for undirected graphs is Christofides' algorithm, which guarantees a
route no more than 50% longer than the best. The local search methods often do better, at the cost
of more time. A small helper measures a route, so the methods can be compared on a tour of all
fourteen cities:

```{python}
def route_length(route):
    return sum(road_net.shortest_path_length(a, b) for a, b in zip(route, route[1:]))


{
    method: route_length(road_net.traveling_salesman(method=method, seed=1))
    for method in ["christofides", "greedy", "simulated_annealing", "threshold_accepting"]
}
```

Simulated annealing finds the shortest tour here, almost 500 km shorter than Christofides', while
the simple greedy method, which always moves to the nearest unvisited stop, is the worst. With
asymmetric costs, such as one-way streets, use a directed graph; there the default is
`"threshold_accepting"`, and `"asadpour"` is also available.

### Steiner trees

A *Steiner tree* connects a given set of *terminal* nodes as cheaply as possible, and may use other
nodes along the way. It is the problem of designing a network: the cheapest set of pipes, cables,
or roads that links a set of sites. [`steiner_tree()`](../reference/Graph.steiner_tree.qmd) finds
an approximate one and returns it as a new graph. Here it connects Paris, Milan, Berlin, and Vienna:

```{python}
tree = road_net.steiner_tree(["Paris", "Milan", "Berlin", "Vienna"])
sorted(names(tree.get_node_ids())), tree.get_edge_df()["weight"].sum()
```

The tree runs south from Paris through Lyon and Geneva to Milan, and from there through Munich and
Prague to Vienna and Berlin, using 2540 km of road. That is far less than the 3700 km of the
[minimum spanning tree](../reference/Graph.minimum_spanning_tree.qmd), which must reach every city.
The Steiner problem is hard to solve exactly, and the method's result is guaranteed to be no more
than twice the optimal length. Here it isn't quite optimal: a tree through Frankfurt and Munich
would use 2430 km. [`directed_steiner_tree()`](../reference/Graph.directed_steiner_tree.qmd) and
[`prize_collecting_steiner_tree()`](../reference/Graph.prize_collecting_steiner_tree.qmd) solve
variants of the problem.

## Paths in other contexts

Path problems turn up throughout the library. The longest path in a directed acyclic graph, which
gives the critical path of a project, is covered in [Directed acyclic graphs](17-dags.qmd).
Centrality measures such as closeness and betweenness are built from shortest paths
([Centrality](13-centrality.qmd)), and flows and cuts generalize disjoint paths
([Connectivity and flows](16-connectivity.qmd)). For Cypher users, `shortestPath()` and
variable-length patterns find paths within a query ([Cypher queries](10-cypher.qmd#path-variables-and-shortest-paths)).
Finally, [`layout_kamada_kawai()`](../reference/Graph.layout_kamada_kawai.qmd) draws a graph so
that the distances in the drawing match the shortest-path distances in the graph (see
[Layouts](23-layouts.qmd)).
